meta.blurb: Four hundred and twenty-three short verses, said to carry the voice of the Buddha, on the mind, anger, happiness and freedom. Walk through the best-loved of them, chapter by chapter, and see why they have been read for more than two thousand years.
meta.bible: The Dhammapada: a Buddhist collection of 423 short verses in 26 chapters, part of the Pali Canon (the Khuddaka Nikaya); the name is often translated as the path of the teaching. Buddha: the awakened teacher who lived in northern India more than two thousand years ago; tradition links the verses to his teaching. Pali: the ancient language of the verses. Dhamma: the teaching. Nibbana: the freedom of a mind at peace. Mara: the tempter who stands for everything that holds the heart in sleep. Arahant: the worthy one who has reached the end of the path. Brahmin: here a truly noble person, one who is noble by conduct, not by birth. Noble Eightfold Path and Four Noble Truths: the core of the teaching. Each beat is one chapter or verse of the book, named by its chapter: Twin Verses, Heedfulness, Mind, Flowers, The Fool, The Wise, The Worthy, Thousands, Evil, Punishment, Old Age, The Self, The World, The Buddha, Happiness, Affection, Anger, Impurity, The Path, The Elephant, Craving, The Monk, The Brahmin. Voice and tone: calm, kind, respectful and plain; verses are paraphrased and never copied; nothing is preached and no other tradition is compared or criticised; no gore.

beats.scene: A monk reads a long palm-leaf manuscript by lamplight in a quiet hall
beats.summary: The Dhammapada is introduced as a collection of 423 verses in 26 chapters.

beats.scene: An ox pulls a heavy cart along a dusty road
beats.summary: Twin Verses: the mind comes first, and an angry mind brings suffering.

beats.scene: A calm woman walks in bright sunlight with her long shadow beside her
beats.summary: Twin Verses: a kind mind brings happiness that follows like a shadow.

beats.scene: Two neighbours at a fence, one holding out an open hand
beats.summary: Twin Verses: hatred is never ended by hatred, only by love.

beats.scene: A crowd argues loudly in a market while one old man watches quietly
beats.summary: Twin Verses: those who remember that everyone must die let their quarrels end.

beats.scene: A monk walks carefully along a mountain path at dawn with open eyes
beats.summary: Heedfulness: careful attention is the path to the deathless; carelessness is the path to death.

beats.scene: A small green island stands firm in a wide flooded river
beats.summary: Heedfulness: by effort and self-control the wise make an island no flood can cover.

beats.scene: A person sits quietly beneath a tree, smiling, with closed eyes
beats.summary: Heedfulness: the one who is careful and meditates finds great happiness.

beats.scene: A craftsman carefully straightens a wooden arrow shaft in his hands
beats.summary: Mind: the wise straighten the trembling mind as a maker of arrows straightens a shaft.

beats.scene: A silver fish thrashes on dry sand beside a river
beats.summary: Mind: the mind struggles like a fish thrown on dry land when it is pulled from its old habits.

beats.scene: A runaway horse slows to a gentle walk beside its rider
beats.summary: Mind: a mind that has been tamed brings happiness.

beats.scene: A mother and father embrace their grown child at the door of a house
beats.summary: Mind: a wrongly directed mind harms us more than an enemy, and a well-directed mind helps us more than a parent.

beats.scene: A bee drinks nectar from a blossom without bending a single petal
beats.summary: Flowers: a bee takes nectar without harming the flower, and the sage passes through a village as gently.

beats.scene: Wind carries petals and scent from a garden along a road toward the town
beats.summary: Flowers: the scent of flowers cannot go against the wind, but the fragrance of the good spreads everywhere.

beats.scene: A tired traveller lies awake at night, staring at a dark ceiling
beats.summary: The Fool: the night is long to the sleepless and the road is long to the weary, and so is life to those who ignore the truth.

beats.scene: A lone traveller walks a long road at sunset with no companion
beats.summary: The Fool: if no better or equal companion can be found, it is better to go on alone than with a fool.

beats.scene: A man laughs gently at himself after dropping his books in the street
beats.summary: The Fool: a fool who knows he is a fool is wise to that extent; a fool who thinks he is wise is the real fool.

beats.scene: A wooden spoon rests in a bowl of hot soup on a kitchen table
beats.summary: The Fool: a fool beside the wise understands nothing, as a spoon cannot taste soup, while a wise person learns quickly.

beats.scene: A friend points out a stain on a man's coat
beats.summary: The Wise: one who points out our faults is like one who shows hidden treasure, and we should follow such a person.

beats.scene: A great grey rock stands firm as wind bends the trees
beats.summary: The Wise: like a solid rock in the wind, the wise are not moved by praise or blame.

beats.scene: A deep clear mountain lake lies perfectly still in the morning light
beats.summary: The Wise: after hearing the teachings, the wise become calm like a clear, deep lake.

beats.scene: A smiling monk stands at the end of a mountain road
beats.summary: The Worthy: for one who has finished the journey there is no sorrow and no fever of the heart.

beats.scene: A calm monk stands still like a pillar as children run past
beats.summary: The Worthy: such a person is patient like the earth, steady like a pillar and clear like a lake without mud.

beats.scene: An old teacher whispers one quiet word to a student in a crowded hall
beats.summary: Thousands: one word of meaning that brings peace is better than a thousand empty words.

beats.scene: A warrior sits alone with closed eyes and his sword laid on the ground
beats.summary: Thousands: the one who conquers himself is a greater conqueror than one who defeats a thousand men.

beats.scene: A girl hurries to carry an old woman's heavy basket
beats.summary: Evil: hurry to do good and keep the mind from evil, or the mind will start to enjoy wrongdoing.

beats.scene: A water jar slowly fills under a roof as drops fall one by one
beats.summary: Evil: even a water jar is filled drop by drop, and so we are filled little by little with good or with evil.

beats.scene: A boy gently stops an older boy from throwing a stone at a bird
beats.summary: Punishment: everyone fears violence and loves life, so we should see ourselves in others and harm no one.

beats.scene: An old royal chariot, worn and faded, stands in a quiet courtyard
beats.summary: Old Age: even royal chariots wear out and the body grows old, but the teaching of the good does not age.

beats.scene: A woman stands alone on a hilltop at sunrise with her arms open
beats.summary: The Self: the self is its own master, and a well-trained self is a rare help.

beats.scene: A man washes his own face and hands in a clear stream at dawn
beats.summary: The Self: we do wrong by ourselves and are made pure by ourselves; no one can purify another.

beats.scene: A sleeper wakes at dawn and rises from bed as light fills the window
beats.summary: The World: rise, do not be careless, and follow the good path, which brings happiness.

beats.scene: A soap bubble floats up and shimmers above a sunlit pond
beats.summary: The World: look upon the world as a bubble or a mirage, and the king of death will not see you.

beats.scene: Three simple lines of text are carved on a stone beside a monastery gate
beats.summary: The Buddha: avoid all evil, do good and purify the mind; patience is the highest discipline.

beats.scene: A hiker stands on a mountain top at dawn, amazed at the view
beats.summary: The Buddha: it is hard to be born human, to live, to hear the true teaching and for a Buddha to arise.

beats.scene: A village of neighbours shares a meal peacefully at one long table
beats.summary: Happiness: let us live happily without hate, even among those who hate.

beats.scene: A farmer rests with bread and water in a quiet field and smiles
beats.summary: Happiness: health is the greatest gift, contentment the greatest wealth, trust the best kinsman and Nibbana the highest happiness.

beats.scene: A child lets go of a kite string and watches the kite rise calmly
beats.summary: Affection: sorrow and fear are born from clinging to what we love; one free of clinging has no sorrow.

beats.scene: A woman answers an angry shouting man with a gentle smile and a gift
beats.summary: Anger: conquer anger by calm, evil by good, the miser by giving and the liar by truth.

beats.scene: A charioteer pulls firmly on the reins to stop a galloping team of horses
beats.summary: Anger: one who checks rising anger like a runaway chariot is a true charioteer.

beats.scene: An old iron sword covered with rust in a dim storeroom
beats.summary: Impurity: rust born from iron eats the iron, as a person's own deeds lead to a bad end.

beats.scene: A wide path with eight stone steps rises through a green hillside
beats.summary: The Path: the best of paths is the Noble Eightfold Path and the best of truths the Four Noble Truths.

beats.scene: A teacher points down a road while a student takes the first step
beats.summary: The Path: we must make the effort ourselves, for the Buddhas only point the way.

beats.scene: Autumn leaves fall from a tree beside a quiet river
beats.summary: The Path: all made things are impermanent, and seeing this with wisdom leads to purity.

beats.scene: A war elephant stands calmly on a dusty field while arrows fall around it
beats.summary: The Elephant: like an elephant in battle, the teacher says he will bear the insults of others.

beats.scene: A lone elephant walks calmly through a quiet forest at dusk
beats.summary: The Elephant: walk with a wise companion if you find one, and if not, walk alone like an elephant in the forest.

beats.scene: A thick green creeper climbs and wraps itself around a tall tree
beats.summary: Craving: craving grows like a creeping vine in the heedless, so dig up its root.

beats.scene: A monk bails water out of a small wooden boat on a calm lake
beats.summary: The Monk: empty your boat and it will go lightly; cut off greed and hatred and reach freedom.

beats.scene: A calm traveller in plain clothes is greeted at a village gate
beats.summary: The Brahmin: one is noble not by matted hair, family or birth, but by truth and righteousness.

beats.scene: Drops of water roll off a lotus leaf on a still pond at sunrise
beats.summary: The Brahmin: the free person clings to no pleasure, like water on a lotus leaf, and the book ends by inviting each reader to walk on.

A1A2: The Dhammapada is a book of short sayings from the Buddhist tradition.
Everything begins in the mind, so an angry mind brings pain.
A kind mind brings happiness, and happiness follows like a shadow.
Hate cannot stop hate, but love can stop it.
Many people forget that life is short, so they fight.
Being awake and careful in every moment leads to true peace.
A wise person makes an island that no flood can cover.
A person who is careful and thinks quietly finds great happiness.
A wise person makes the mind straight as a man makes an arrow straight.
A fish pulled from water jumps and shakes on dry ground.
A mind that is trained and calm brings real happiness.
A wrong thought can hurt you more than an enemy can.
A bee takes honey from a flower and does not hurt it.
The scent of flowers goes with the wind, but goodness goes everywhere.
The night is long for a person who cannot sleep.
It is better to walk alone than with a foolish friend.
A fool who knows he is a fool is already a little wise.
A spoon sits in the soup all day but never tastes it.
Be glad of a person who shows you your mistakes.
Praise and blame cannot move the wise, as wind cannot move rock.
After hearing the teaching, the wise become calm like a clear lake.
For the one who has finished the journey, there is no more sorrow.
He is patient like the earth and does not get angry.
One word that brings peace is better than a thousand empty words.
The greatest winner is the person who wins over himself.
Do good things quickly, before the mind turns to bad things.
Drop by drop, an empty water pot slowly becomes full.
Everyone is afraid of pain, so do not hurt other people.
Even a king's fine chariot wears out, and so does the body.
You are your own master, so take good care of yourself.
We make ourselves pure; no one else can do it for us.
Wake up, do not be lazy, and follow the good path.
See the world as a bubble, and nothing will trouble you.
Do no wrong, do good, and make your mind clean.
Being a person is rare, and hearing the teaching is rare.
Let us live happily and hate no one, even among haters.
Good health is the best gift, and being content is the best wealth.
Too much clinging to people brings sorrow and fear.
Beat anger with kindness, and beat lies with truth.
A wise person stops anger the way a driver stops a runaway cart.
Rust grows from iron and slowly eats the iron itself.
Of all the paths, the Eightfold Path is the best.
You must make the effort yourself, because teachers only show the way.
All made things change, and seeing this brings wisdom and peace.
I will bear insults like an elephant bears arrows in a battle.
If you find no good friend, walk alone like an elephant in the forest.
Wanting more and more grows like a weed in a careless mind.
Empty the boat, and it will move lightly across the water.
We are noble because of our actions, not because of our birth.
The free person does not cling, like water on a lotus leaf.
B1B2: The Dhammapada is a collection of 423 short verses arranged in 26 chapters. They are part of the Pali Canon, an early collection of Buddhist scriptures, and Buddhists everywhere have loved them for centuries.
The first chapter says that the mind comes before everything we do. If we speak or act with an angry mind, suffering follows us, as a wheel follows the ox.
The next verse shows the same law working in the opposite direction, toward joy. When we speak or act with a clear and kind mind, happiness follows us like a shadow that never leaves.
One of the best-known verses says that hatred is never ended by hatred. Only love can end it, and the verse calls this an old and lasting truth.
Another verse says that many people forget that we must all die one day. Those who do remember it find that their quarrels begin to end.
The second chapter praises heedfulness, which means paying close attention to what we think and do. It says that attention leads to the deathless, while those who are careless are as good as dead.
By effort, care and self-control, says the Dhammapada, a wise person can build an island. No flood will ever be able to cover it.
The chapter tells us not to be careless or to chase pleasures all day. A person who is careful and who thinks quietly finds great happiness.
The third chapter is about the mind, which it calls restless and hard to guard. Just as a maker of arrows straightens each arrow, the wise person slowly straightens the mind.
The mind, says the Dhammapada, is like a fish that has been thrown onto dry land. It twists and shakes whenever we try to pull it out of its old habits, but we should keep trying.
The mind is hard to hold, because it flies wherever it wishes. But a mind that has been tamed and trained brings happiness to its owner.
An enemy can do us harm, and so can a person who hates us. Yet a badly directed mind harms us even more, and a well-directed mind helps us more than our own parents can.

The fourth chapter is called Flowers, and one of its pictures shows a bee at work. The bee takes its nectar and flies away without harming the flower, and the wise walk through villages in the same gentle way.
The scent of flowers, or even of sandalwood, cannot travel against the wind. However, the fragrance of a good person spreads in every direction, even against the wind.
The fifth chapter is about the fool, a person who does not learn from life. The night seems long to the sleepless and the road long to the tired, and so is life to those who ignore the truth.
If a traveller cannot find a companion who is better or at least equal, he should go on alone. A fool cannot be a good companion on the road.
A fool who knows that he is a fool is, to that extent, already wise. The fool who thinks he is wise, however, is the one who is truly called a fool.
A spoon may sit in a bowl of soup for a lifetime and never taste it. In the same way, a fool who lives near a wise person may never understand the teaching.
Imagine that a stranger shows you where a great treasure is buried. The Dhammapada says that a friend who shows us our faults is just as valuable, and that we should follow him.
A solid rock is not shaken by the wind, however hard it blows. In the same way, a wise person is not moved by either praise or blame.
Like a deep lake that is clear and still, the wise grow calm after they have heard the teachings. Their minds become quiet, and in that stillness they see things as they really are.
The seventh chapter describes the arahant, a person who has reached the end of the path. For him the journey is over, and he is free from sorrow and from every kind of bond.
Such a person is patient like the earth, which does not resent anyone who walks across it. He is steady like a pillar, and he is like a lake without mud, calm and clear.
The eighth chapter is called Thousands, and it compares large numbers with small ones. Better than a thousand empty words, it says, is a single word that brings peace to whoever hears it.
Imagine a man who defeats a thousand thousand men in battle, one after another. The verse says that someone who conquers himself is a far greater winner than he is.
The ninth chapter tells us to hurry to do good and to hold the mind back from evil. If we are slow to do good, it warns, the mind will begin to enjoy doing wrong.
Never think lightly of wrongdoing by saying that it will not come back to you. A water jar is filled drop by drop, and so we are filled, little by little, with good or with evil.
The tenth chapter says that everyone is afraid of violence, and that everyone loves life. If we imagine ourselves in the place of others, we will not wish to hurt any living being.
The eleventh chapter speaks about growing old, and it does so without fear. Even a splendid royal chariot wears out, and so does the body, but the teaching of the good never grows old.
The twelfth chapter is called The Self, and it begins with a strong claim. It says that each of us is our own master, and that a well-trained self is a rare and precious help.

By ourselves we do wrong, and by ourselves we become unclean, says the verse. In the same way, we make ourselves pure, because purity and impurity belong to each person and no one can cleanse another.
The thirteenth chapter, called The World, begins with a loud call to wake up. It tells us to get up, to be careful and to follow the good path, which brings happiness.
The verse tells us to look upon the world as we would look at a bubble or a mirage. It says that the king of death cannot find a person who sees the world like this.
One verse in the chapter on the Buddha is often called a short summary of the whole teaching. It says that we should avoid all evil, do good, and purify our own minds.
The same chapter says that it is hard to be born as a human being, and hard to live a mortal life. It is also hard to hear the true teaching, and hard for a Buddha to appear in the world.

The fifteenth chapter is called Happiness, and its first verses are about freedom from hate. It says that we can live happily without hatred even among people who hate, and without worry even among those who worry.
Health is the greatest gift, says the Dhammapada, and contentment is the greatest wealth. A trusted person is the best of relatives, and freedom, called Nibbana, is the greatest happiness.
The sixteenth chapter, called Affection, says that sorrow and fear are born from clinging to what we love. A person who is wholly free from clinging has no sorrow, and so he has nothing to fear.
The seventeenth chapter, which is about anger, tells us to defeat anger with calm. We should overcome evil with good, a miser with giving, and a liar with the truth.
Anger can rise like a chariot that has begun to run away with its driver. The person who stops it quickly, says the verse, is a true charioteer, and the others only hold the reins.
Rust is born from iron, but then it slowly eats the iron away. In the same way, our own bad deeds lead us toward a sad end.
The twentieth chapter, called The Path, names the best of all paths. It says that the best path is the Noble Eightfold Path and that the best truths are the Four Noble Truths.
The verse says that we ourselves must make the effort, because the Buddhas only point the way. Those who walk the path and keep their minds steady will be freed from the bonds of Mara, the tempter.
All made things change and pass away, and a person who sees this with wisdom grows tired of suffering. This clear seeing, says the verse, is the path that leads to purity.

The twenty-third chapter is named after the elephant, an animal that was trained for battle. Just as an elephant in battle endures the arrows that strike it, says the verse, I will bear the insults of others.
If you find a wise and good friend, walk with him, happy and thoughtful. If you find none, walk alone like an elephant in the forest, doing no harm and wanting little.
The twenty-fourth chapter is about craving, which grows like a creeping vine in the heedless. Dig up its roots, says the verse, as a gardener digs up a weed, so that it cannot grow again and again.
The twenty-fifth chapter is about the monk, who has left home to follow the path. It tells him to empty his boat, because a boat that is empty moves lightly, and to cut off greed and hatred.
The last chapter describes the brahmin, a word that here means a truly noble person. A person is not made noble by long hair, by family or by birth, but by truth and righteousness.

The last verses describe a person who clings to nothing, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. That person has put down every heavy burden, and the book ends by inviting each reader to walk toward the same peace.
C1C2: The Dhammapada is a collection of 423 short verses, set in 26 chapters, that belongs to the Pali Canon, one of the earliest bodies of Buddhist scripture. Its name is often translated as the path of the teaching, and tradition links its verses to the words of the Buddha, who lived in northern India more than two thousand years ago. Each verse is meant to be read slowly and carried into daily life, so this retelling takes its best-loved lines in the order of the chapters.

The very first verses of the Dhammapada declare that mind is the forerunner of all things, and that every deed grows out of a thought. Speak or act with a troubled and angry mind, they warn, and suffering will follow as surely as the wheel of a cart follows the hoof of the ox that draws it. The lesson is not meant as a threat but as a plain observation, for what we think quietly today shapes what we do loudly tomorrow.

The second verse mirrors the first and turns the same law toward the light, so that the reader may see both of its faces. When a person speaks or acts with a pure and gentle mind, joy follows as faithfully as a shadow that never leaves its owner. Together the two verses set out the central idea of the whole book: our inner state is the seed, and our life is the harvest.

In a verse that has been quoted for many centuries, the teaching says that hatred is never calmed by hatred in this world. It is calmed only by love, and this, the verse adds, is an ancient law that does not change with time or place. Anyone who has answered anger with anger and watched a quarrel grow will recognise the truth of it at once.

Many people quarrel as though life were endless, the verse observes, and they do not remember that everyone must one day die. Those who do remember it, who hold that plain fact steadily in view, find that their quarrels begin to lose their force. It is a sober thought, yet it is offered as a way to a lighter and more peaceful heart.

The second chapter is a praise of heedfulness, a word that means keeping the mind alert and caring about what one thinks, says and does. Attention, it declares, is the path to the deathless, while carelessness is the road to death, and the careless are as good as dead while they still breathe. The wise understand this difference clearly, and so they take delight in staying awake.

Through steady effort, careful attention and self-control, the verse says, a wise person can make for himself an island that no flood can overwhelm. The image is memorable because the floods in this teaching are the troubles of life, the waves of anger, fear and loss that sweep over everyone sooner or later. Only the person who has built such an island within can stand on it and remain safe.

Do not give yourself to carelessness, the chapter says, and do not wear yourself out in the chase after sensual pleasures. A person who is attentive and who sits quietly in meditation, by contrast, arrives at great and lasting happiness. The difference is between a joy that must be bought again every day and a joy that is simply there once the mind is still.

The third chapter turns to the mind itself, which it describes as trembling, unsteady and hard to guard or to hold in check. Just as a maker of arrows patiently straightens each shaft, the verse says, a wise person straightens the mind. It is a craftsman's task, done a little each day, and it asks for patience far more than for force.

Another verse compares the mind to a fish pulled from its pool and thrown onto dry ground, where it twists and shivers in distress. So the mind struggles, the Dhammapada says, when a person first tries to pull it out of its old habits and into stillness. Anyone who has tried to sit quietly for five minutes will know exactly what the fish is feeling.

The mind is hard to hold and light as a leaf, the verse says, and it settles wherever it wishes, whether or not that place is good for us. A mind that has been tamed, however, is a source of happiness that nothing else can give. For this reason the teaching asks us to train the mind with the same care that a rider gives to a spirited horse.

An enemy may harm an enemy, the Dhammapada notes, and a hater may harm the one he hates, but a mind turned in the wrong direction does far greater damage than either. In the same way, a well-directed mind can do us more good than even a mother or a father could. Everything, in other words, depends on where the mind is pointed, and that is the one thing we can change from within.

In the chapter called Flowers, the teaching offers a picture of a bee that visits a blossom, takes its nectar and flies away without damaging its colour or its scent. The sage, the verse says, should go through the village in just the same way, taking what he needs and leaving the place unharmed. It is a lesson in gentleness that asks for no grand gestures, only for a careful and light touch.

The perfume of flowers, even of sandalwood or jasmine, cannot travel against the wind, and so its reach is limited by the weather. The fragrance of a good person, however, drifts in every direction and even against the wind, because kindness is remembered long after a person has left the room. It is, the verse seems to say, the one perfume that is worth wearing.

The fifth chapter turns to the fool, by which it means anyone who does not learn from his own mistakes. The night is long for the sleepless, it says, and the road is long for the weary, and so the round of life is long for those who have never grasped the true teaching. Ignorance, in this telling, is not wickedness but tiredness, a weight that makes every step heavier than it needs to be.

If a traveller cannot find a companion who is wiser than himself, or at least as wise, the verse advises him to continue firmly on his own. There is no friendship to be had with a fool, it says, and a bad companion will hold a person back far more than the road itself ever could. The advice is not unkind, only honest about how strongly the company we keep shapes the people we become.

A fool who knows that he is a fool, the Dhammapada says, is for that reason wise, because the first step toward learning is to admit that there is something to learn. The fool who believes himself to be wise, on the other hand, deserves to be called a fool indeed. Pride is the one thing that closes every door, and humility is the key that opens them again.

Even if a fool spends his whole life in the company of a wise person, the verse says, he will understand nothing of the teaching, just as a spoon never tastes the soup it stirs. A person of understanding, by contrast, needs only a moment beside the wise to grasp what is being said, as the tongue knows the flavour of the soup at once. Learning, we are reminded, depends less on who stands near us than on how open we are.

The chapter on the wise begins with an unusual image: someone who points out your faults, it says, is like a person who shows you where a hidden treasure lies. Follow such a person, the verse urges, for it will go better and never worse for anyone who does so. Few of us enjoy being corrected, yet the one who corrects us kindly is giving us something that flattery never could.

As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, so the wise are not moved by praise or by blame, however loudly either one is spoken. They have learned that the opinions of others pass like weather, and that peace depends on something steadier than applause. Such calm is not coldness; it is the freedom of someone who no longer needs to be told who he is.

When the wise have listened to the teachings, the verse says, their minds become tranquil like a deep lake that is clear and undisturbed. Water that is stirred up shows only mud, but water that is left alone reveals every stone at the bottom. In the same way, a quiet mind sees its own situation plainly, and nothing in it has to be hidden or feared.

The seventh chapter describes the arahant, the worthy one who has travelled the whole path to its end and is free from sorrow in every direction. For such a person, the verse says, the fever of the heart has gone, and the chains that once held him have fallen away. It is a portrait of complete freedom, offered less as a prize that is out of reach than as a direction in which every reader may begin to walk.

Such a person is patient like the earth, which does not resent those who tread upon it, and steady like a firm pillar that no storm can shift. He is also like a lake from which all the mud has settled, clear to the bottom and calm on the surface. For one who lives in this way, the verse concludes, there are no more restless wanderings, because there is nowhere left he needs to run.

The eighth chapter, called Thousands, sets large numbers against small ones in order to show that what matters is quality and not quantity. Better than a thousand empty words, it says, is a single word of meaning that brings peace to the one who hears it. Anyone who has been comforted by a short and honest sentence in a time of need will understand why this verse has lasted so long.

Even if a man were to defeat a thousand times a thousand men in battle, the verse says, the one who conquers only himself is the greatest of all conquerors. Armies can be beaten and cities taken, but the habits of one's own heart are a much harder country to win. It is a surprising kind of heroism, one that is fought alone, in silence, and without any audience at all.

Make haste to do good, the ninth chapter urges, and hold your mind back from evil, for the mind that is slow to act kindly soon starts to take pleasure in wrongdoing. Good intentions that are put off until tomorrow tend to fade by the evening, while an unkind impulse needs no encouragement at all. The remedy offered here is simple: act on the good thought at once, before it has time to cool.

Do not think lightly of wrongdoing, the verse warns, by telling yourself that it will never come back to you, for even a water jar is filled drop by drop. In the same way, a fool is filled with evil a little at a time, and the following verse says that the wise are filled with goodness just as gradually. Small deeds repeated every day, in other words, are the true builders of character.

Everyone trembles before violence and everyone fears death, says the tenth chapter, and life is dear to all. A person who truly sees himself in other beings, it concludes, will neither strike nor cause another to strike. The rule is as old as it is simple, and it asks for nothing more than an honest effort of the imagination.

Even the splendid chariots of kings wear out in time, the eleventh chapter observes, and the body too must grow old. The teaching of the good, however, does not grow old, for the wise pass it from one to another across the years. The verse speaks of age without fear and offers a quiet consolation: what we love and understand can outlast the body that carried it.

The twelfth chapter makes a bold claim about responsibility: the self is its own master, and nobody else can take that place, however much we might wish them to. When a person has trained himself well, the verse adds, he has found a helper that is difficult to find anywhere in the world. It places the work of change squarely in each reader's hands, which is both a burden and a great encouragement.

It is by oneself that wrong is done, the verse says, and by oneself that a person is made unclean. It is likewise by oneself that wrong is left undone and one is made pure, for purity and impurity belong to each person alone. No one, however loving or learned, can purify another, and that is why the work must always begin at home.

The thirteenth chapter, which is called The World, opens with a call like the sound of a bell in the early morning. Rise up and do not be careless, it says, but follow the good path with all your heart, for whoever walks it lives happily both in this world and in the next. The verse does not frighten the reader; it only invites him to wake, as one wakes on a bright morning, and to begin.

Look upon the world as you would look upon a bubble or a mirage, the verse advises, and the king of death will not see you. The image is not meant to make life seem worthless, but to loosen the grip of the person who clutches at everything as if it were permanent. Whoever sees how lightly the world is made, it implies, can walk through it without fear of losing what was never fixed in the first place.

In the chapter called The Buddha, one verse is often described as a summary of the whole teaching in a single breath. Avoid all evil, it says, do what is good, and cleanse your own mind, and this is what the awakened ones have taught. Beside it stands another line praising patience as the highest discipline, as if to say that all three tasks will take a very long time.

Four things are difficult, the chapter says: to be born as a human being, to live out the life of a mortal, to hear the true teaching, and for an awakened one to appear in the world. The list is meant to make us feel how rare and precious this present chance is, rather than to make us anxious. If you are alive and listening to the teaching, then you already hold a gift that is far from common.

The fifteenth chapter is called Happiness, and it begins by describing how happily we may live without hatred, even among people who hate. We may live free of sickness among the sick, the verse continues, and free of anxiety among the anxious, as long as we do not let their state become ours. It is a picture of happiness that does not wait for the world around us to improve.

Health is the greatest of gifts, the verse says, and contentment is the greatest of riches, for a person who has enough lacks nothing. A trusted friend is the best of relatives, and Nibbana, the freedom of a mind at peace, is the highest happiness there is. The list is a quiet challenge to the usual order of things, since most of us spend our best years chasing items that are placed far lower.

The sixteenth chapter says that sorrow and fear are born from affection, and that a person who is wholly free of it has no grief and nothing to fear. Teachers explain that this points to clinging, a grasping love that cannot bear to lose what it holds, and not to love itself in its open and generous form. The teaching asks us to hold dear things gently, so that when they pass, they do not take our peace with them.

Conquer anger by the absence of anger, says the seventeenth chapter, and conquer evil by good, for no fault is cured by feeding it. Conquer the miser with generosity, and conquer the liar with the truth, for each fault is best met by its opposite. It is a strategy of patience rather than of force, and it works because it leaves the other person with nothing to push against.

Anger rises like a chariot that has begun to run away with its driver, and most of us are carried along behind it. Whoever can check it in the moment of its rising, the verse says, deserves to be called a true charioteer, while others merely hold the reins. To master the feeling at its first stirring, before it has gathered speed, is the whole of the skill.

The eighteenth chapter, on impurity, compares wrongdoing to rust, which is born from iron and yet slowly eats the very iron from which it came. A person's own deeds, it says, carry him toward a sorrowful end, so the harm does not come from outside but grows within the one who does wrong. The chapter names ignorance as the worst stain of all, because a mind that cannot see its own rust has no reason to clean it.

The twentieth chapter, called The Path, names the best of all roads as the Noble Eightfold Path, and the best of all truths as the Four Noble Truths. Dispassion is called the best of states, and the one who sees clearly the best of human beings. This path, the verse concludes, is the only one that leads to the purifying of insight, and the reader is urged to follow it.

You yourselves must make the effort, says the twentieth chapter, for the Buddhas can only point the way. Those who enter the path and keep their minds steady in meditation will be freed from the bonds of Mara, the tempter who stands for everything that holds the heart in sleep. No teacher, however great, can walk the road in anyone's place, and this verse says so with beautiful honesty.

All made things are impermanent, the verse says, and when a person sees this with true insight, he begins to turn away from suffering. The same chapter adds that all things are without a lasting self, and that seeing this too is the road to purity. The thought is hard at first, like cold water, but those who accept it often find that the grip of worry is loosened.

The twenty-third chapter takes its name from the elephant, which in ancient times was trained to carry kings into battle and to stand firm while arrows fell around it. Just as such an elephant endures every shot, the verse says in the voice of the teacher, so shall I endure the harsh words of others, for the world is full of people who speak carelessly. The chapter adds that a tamed elephant is a fine thing, but that the person who has tamed himself is finer still.

If you find a wise and steady companion, the chapter says, walk with him, glad and thoughtful, and overcome every danger on the way. If you find none, then go on alone like an elephant in the great forest, or like a king who has left a conquered country behind him. There is companionship in the first case and freedom in the second, and the verse sees nothing to fear in either.

The twenty-fourth chapter is about craving, which in the heedless grows like a creeping vine that wraps itself around everything it touches. Whoever is overcome by this fierce thirst finds his sorrows multiplying, the verse says, as grass grows quickly after the rain. The remedy it offers is to dig up the root, so that craving cannot rise again and again like a weed that has only been cut back.

The twenty-fifth chapter is addressed to the monk, the one who has left home to follow the path, but its advice is useful to anyone. Bail out the water from your boat, it says, for when it is emptied it will go lightly across the lake. If you cut off greed and hatred, the weight that slows you will be gone, and you will reach freedom with far less effort than you now imagine.

The last chapter describes the brahmin, a word that in this book means a truly noble person, and it makes an important point at once. One does not become noble by matted hair, by family or by birth, the verse says, but by truth and righteousness. In this way the teaching places worth in conduct rather than rank, and it draws a portrait of a man who is free in the heart, not merely in name.

In its closing verses the Dhammapada describes the one who clings to no pleasure, like a drop of water that rolls from a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed that slips from the point of a needle. Such a person has put down every heavy burden and moves through the world without fear, anger or grasping. The book ends where it began, with the mind, and leaves each reader to walk the path in his own way and at his own pace.
